title: Positive Framing, Part 1: Live in the Now
author: The Teach Like a Champion Team
source: Teach Like a Champion on Substack, December 14, 2025
summary: Timed for the wiggly last week before break, Live in the Now reverses the reflex to correct by looking backward and instead gives the smallest, clearest next step toward success. Specific bite-sized directives preserve trust and dignity while anchoring students to forward momentum. The frame is actionable and motivating rather than backward-looking; in a week when routines fray, the teacher who substitutes what-you-want-to-see-next for what-just-went-wrong builds momentum without judgment and delivers a model for rebuilding routine after the January break.
points: When a class feels off, the instinct is backward-facing correction (naming the misstep); forward-facing directives (describing the next action) are more motivating and preserve trust.
Shrink-the-change instructions give specific, bite-sized directions that communicate belief in the child's ability to follow through and let them re-enter learning with dignity intact.
Phrasing choices that describe what you want to see next rather than naming what just went wrong look micro but work macro, especially in high-energy weeks when routines fray.
Anchoring students to the next visible action builds momentum without moral judgment, a discipline that transfers to January routine rebuilding after break.
The core move operates on a simple principle: describe what you want to see next, not what you just saw go wrong.
quotes: For many teachers, this coming week can be one of the trickiest of the year. Students are excited for winter break, the energy in the room is shifting, and attention can feel elastic.
When classes feel wiggly, it's easy to focus on what just went wrong. We've talked about this. Why aren't you on page 12? But looking backward rarely gets students (or us) where we need to go.

Live in the Now shifts the frame away from the misstep and toward what should happen next. It's forward-facing, actionable, and motivating.” “The core move is simple: give the smallest, clearest step toward success. Instead of 'You should be taking notes,' try something like: 'Pencil in hand, ready to capture this next example.

Students respond to specific, bite-sized directions, especially during high-energy weeks. Clear next steps reduce resistance, refocus attention, and communicate our belief in their ability to follow through.
When you describe the positive next action, rather than the mistake, you change the story students see. Great coaching is about always describing what you want to see next.
No frustration. No backward-looking critique. Just clear, doable next steps. And because the direction is specific, students know exactly how to be successful right now.

Positive Framing works because it preserves trust. Even small choices in phrasing, especially during potentially messy weeks, signal belief: You can do this. I'm here to help you get there.” Archived from Teach Like a Champion on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
